If there is a religious belief at home, be sincere and respectful, devotedly recite the Buddha's name, pray for blessings, as doing so will greatly help in eliminating sexual misconduct.

Story 4

A young man looked like he was only 11 or 12 years old, but he dressed completely like an adult. From his hairstyle to his clothes, everything was very fashionable. The only issue was his curved waist and hunched back, with a gloomy demeanor, showing no vitality and a heavily weary spirit. Master Tan asked him what problem he wanted to address. He said his back hurt, his legs ached, and he couldn't straighten his waist.

Master Tan asked:

– How old are you this year?

Answer:

– 22 years old

Asks again:

– When did you start playing on the computer?

Answer:

– Since I was about ten years old.

Asks:

– Do you know what your illness is? Do you know why your body is currently in such poor condition?

Answer:

– I know a little; it's because I played computer games.

Master Tan said thoughtfully:

– It's not just simply playing computer games! Be honest, over these past few years, how many things have you watched that you shouldn't have? How many chaotic thoughts are in your mind? Those habits have damaged your kidneys, your body can't develop properly, and there isn't enough nutrition provided to your body, so your current appearance is only like that of an 11 or 12-year-old child. Right now, if you still don't know how to stop before the abyss, even more frightening consequences are waiting for you!

The young man, after hearing that, could only bow his head without saying another word.

Master Tan then asked:

– Do you want to get better? If you want, I will tell you the method, but if you don’t want to get better, I have no way. Right now, the only person who can save you is yourself!

The young man nodded and said:

– I want to.

Master Tan gently said:

– First, absolutely do not touch the computer, no more playing on the computer, and no more watching those chaotic things, can you do that?

The boy nodded his head.

– Second, in your mind, absolutely do not think about those chaotic things anymore, this point must be accomplished, can you do that?

He nodded, but his attitude was not very firm. The attendant master, seeing his hesitant response, sighed and said:

– Those chaotic things on the internet are really harmful, causing you to lose the most precious essence in your body!

I’ll tell you, a person's kidney essence is connected to the bone marrow, and a person's bone marrow is connected to the cerebrospinal fluid. Moreover, during puberty, the development of the human body relies on kidney energy. Your current body shape is like that of an 11- or 12-year-old child; your body hasn’t fully reached puberty. That’s because the essence in your body has long been depleted, and without nourishment, how can your body grow? How can it mature?

Tuesday, from now on, try to change your bad habits and that unhealthy lifestyle; it definitely must be improved. Go to bed early and get up early every day, persist in exercising, take opportunities to do more public service work, and when at home, help your parents with housework. Can you do that?

You nodded. Master Tan saw that your attitude was not very determined, and immediately said to you:

– Ah, I’ve already told you my method, as for how to do it, that’s up to you; destiny lies in your hands, you have to arrange it yourself!

The tutor turned back and said to your father:

– You only know how to spoil your children. If they want a computer, you immediately buy them one. But do you know what the kids are doing once they close the door to their room, what they’re looking at? With children, they ask for something and you immediately give it; but how about towards the parents?

Is this fulfilling filial duty? Your children are not good because you are crazy about human relationships, only know how to love the young, but do not know how to be filial to your parents. Your energy is all spent on your children, just like watering flowers without watering the roots, only worrying about the buds; how can there be good descendants?

Source: Lê Tơ Hồng

tieu_de: A Hundred Methods
tom_tat: (Table of 100 mistakes, used for self-examination of mistakes and daily repentance) 1. Daily activities are not normal.
noi_dung:
BAKED FRUIT METHOD

(Table of 100 faults, used for self-reflection and daily repentance)

1. Daily living is not normal.

2. Clothing and appearance are not proper or clean.

3. Spitting or throwing trash carelessly, eating while walking.

4. Seeing trash thrown on the ground but not picking it up when convenient.

5. Personal hygiene or home is dirty and messy, habits of uncleanliness have not changed.

6. Also has bad habits such as smoking, drinking alcohol, chewing betel ...

7. Does not comply with public order, drives without following traffic laws.

8. Goes to inappropriate places.

9. Does not fulfill duties at work, lacks respect for the profession.

10. Lives without a cheerful spirit, has low efficiency in work or study.

11. Does not get along with others, lacks team spirit.

12. When meeting neighbors, colleagues, or acquaintances, cannot yet smile and greet.

13. Cannot yet be friendly with relatives, harmonize with neighbors, or watch over and help each other.

14. When encountering disabled people, the elderly, or children, cannot help.

15. Normally likes to watch TV, newspapers, magazines...

16. Watching films, pictures, books, newspapers... with sexual content, or actions that violate sexual morality.

17. Abnormal interactions between men and women.

18. Yesterday made a mistake but has not corrected it today, repeating bad habits.

19. Killing or harming sentient beings.

20. Seeking enjoyment in eating, dressing, living, and traveling.

21. Stealing or taking anything from others without their consent.

22. Participating in vegetarian meals, merit meals, or on the Buddha's and Bodhisattvas' birthdays without being able to abstain from meat or sexual misconduct.

23. Being unable to eat vegetarian for a normal breakfast.

24. Wasting grains or food.

25. Not being frugal, living an extravagant life, being wasteful.

26. Meeting images of Buddha, Bodhisattva, or monastics without yet cultivating a sincere heart to greet or pay respects.

27. Not being filial to parents (causing parents worry or anger)

28. Not respecting the master, not being loyal to siblings or friends.

29. Having discord at home or between husband and wife.

30. For those who are not sincere, their attitude is arrogant and conceited.

31. In dealing with others, they are not trustworthy or do not keep promises to people.

32. In dealing with others, they still like to take advantage of others.

33. In dealing with others, they are still afraid of others taking advantage of them or still calculate gains and losses.

34. In dealing with others, even in learning Buddhism and practicing, they still have a mind of looking for favors and conditions.

35. In dealing with others, they still have feelings of suspicion, doubt, and jealousy.

36. Morning and evening Dharma sessions cannot yet be completed perfectly on time.

37. Reciting the Buddha's name nine times a day (Ten Recitations Practice) has not yet been accomplished.

38. Generally unable to grasp time for practice and study, letting time pass in vain.

39. In practicing and studying the Dharma, the mind is not focused, and recitation is not consistent.

40. Learning and practicing Buddhism is done with laxity, lacking perseverance, or a mind arises to retreat and fear.

41. Encountering opportunities where one should act but has not acted, or should let go but has not let go.

42. Helping others who do not have the courage to move forward.

43. Helping those who do wrong; seeing others anxious and fearful but not comforting them.

44. Sentient beings with affinities with the true Dharma but have not actively guided them.

45. Doing business using unscrupulous schemes, improper methods to seek profit.

46. Having behaviors and attitudes of receiving benefits without effort, such as speculation, gambling, engaging in illegal activities, not conducting legitimate business...

47. Language and actions that are improper, coarse, and rude.

48. Speaking harsh, evil, and filthy words.

49. Speaking in a rude way, with an improper attitude in conversation.

50. Using false words to deceive others.

51. Engaging in meaningless chatter or involving oneself in useless matters.

52. Being careless with speech, speaking many words without any being useful.

53. Talking in a boastful manner or wanting to stand out more than others.

54. Speaking and behaving dishonestly, or causing harm to others, without feeling remorse.

55. Talking at an inappropriate speed or volume.

56. Speaking at the wrong time or place, or having the habit of interrupting rudely.

57. Speaking deceitfully or sowing discord, gossiping about right and wrong.

58. Discussing the rights and wrongs of others, freely criticizing others.

59. Speaking one thing with the mouth but thinking another in the heart, inconsistent inside and out.

60. Slandering the Three Jewels, destroying the teaching of the true Dharma.

61. Saying beautiful words to deceive others, using flowery speech and cunning words to seduce others.

62. Liking to hear praises, feeling joy after hearing them; hating to hear contrary words, feeling sorrow, annoyance, and anger after hearing them, unable to self-reflect.

63. Having a hasty, restless temperament, unable to bear temporary anger.

64. Narrow-minded, unable to tolerate or forgive others.

65. Reckless, whimsical, doing as one pleases.

66. Arouse thoughts driven by self-interest.

67. Harboring hidden ill intentions to harm others.

68. Presents of evil conditions arise before the eyes, the mind generates affliction, harbors resentment, or thinks of revenge.

69. Seeing with the eyes or hearing with the ears something slightly unfavorable, immediately gives rise to an unhappy mind.

70. Seeing people, objects, or events, there is still a feeling of displeasure.

71. Being greedy and miserly, unwilling to give, or giving and then feeling regret.

72. Not knowing fate, not accepting fate, and starting to desire beyond one's own lot.

73. When favorable circumstances appear or one surpasses others, the mind generates arrogance or a conceited attitude.

74. When adverse circumstances occur or things go against desires, blaming heaven and others or despising oneself arises.

75. When feeling dissatisfied, one immediately sighs, complains, or becomes angry.

76. Feeling envious when seeing others succeed, and feeling pleased when seeing others meet difficulties.

77. Seeing good people or good deeds but not yet being able to feel joy in the heart.

78. Still attached to personal relationships, reputation, and profit, still feeling worry about gain and loss.

79. Desires for the five senses and six worldly matters are still strong, and daily activities pass without a sense of steadiness.

80. Right and wrong arise in a way that makes it impossible to promptly observe and face with an ordinary mind.

81. Falling into the fault of seeing small virtuous deeds but not doing them, and seeing small evil deeds but doing them.

82. Unable to often think of one's own faults, but instead often see the faults of others.

83. False thoughts and afflictions arise, yet there is no way to promptly contemplate and replace them with the Buddha's name.

84. In ordinary times, the mind lacks correct mindfulness, with false thoughts and miscellaneous thoughts scattered everywhere.

85. Today, the mind is distant from the Dharma, daily activities are experienced in confusion or unrest.

86. Towards parents, teachers, and karmic virtuous friends, there is no feeling of gratitude.

87. Has not yet been able to see the merits of others to learn from them, nor see the faults of others to reflect on oneself.

88. Has not yet been able to constantly feel shame and daily engage in repentance.

89. In daily activities, has not yet been able to face things with a neutral and equal mind.

90. Has not been able to sincerely recite Buddha's name early in the morning and cultivate a joyful mind, and to maintain a pure mind throughout the day while reciting Buddha's name.

91. When talking with others, has not been able to use a gentle expression, soft words, humble attitude, and sincerity.

92. Has not been able to use a sincere and respectful heart to treat everyone.

93. Has not been able to maintain a gentle, good, and compassionate mind.

94. Has not been able to practice the virtues: creating merit, cherishing merit, and being frugal.

95. Has not yet practiced virtue: being humble inside, polite and yielding outside.

96. Has not yet practiced: what one does not wish for oneself, do not give to others.

97. Has not yet practiced: be strict with oneself, be tolerant with others.

98. Has not yet practiced: endure adversity when it comes, and when favorable conditions come, do not generate greed.

99. Has not yet practiced the compassionate spirit of a Bodhisattva, cannot bear to eat the flesh of living beings.

100. Have not yet achieved not contending with others, not seeking from the world.

tieu_de: WHY DOES THE SAME MANTRA have MANY DIFFERENT VERSIONS?
tom_tat: Ken Bi: -Hello Mr. Quang Tu, please may I ask, I have read the Great Compassion Mantra, but I noticed, the same sentence is recorded as: “Tat Ba A Tha Dau Thau Bang”, while another version records it as “Tat Ba A Tha Dau Du Bang”
noi_dung:
WHY DOES THE SAME SPELL have MANY DIFFERENT VERSIONS?

Ken Bi:

-Hello Mr. Quang Tử, may I ask you, I have read the Great Compassion Mantra, but I noticed that the same sentence has one version recorded as: “Tát Bà A Tha Đậu Thâu Bằng”, and another version recorded as “Tát Bà A Tha Đậu Du Bằng“

So may I ask you which of these two sentences is correct? Also, when chanting the Great Compassion Mantra in Vietnamese versus Sanskrit, which version is better? I haven't read Sanskrit yet but I heard that Sanskrit is more accurate, is that true? Thank you!

Quang Tử :

– Dear friend, the Buddha was originally an Indian who lived over 2,500 years ago, so when teaching mantras, He used the ancient Indian language, which is Sanskrit.

Later, when the great masters, disciples of the Buddha, spread the sutras and mantras from India to other countries, they encountered a problem: people in other countries like China, Japan, Vietnam… found it very difficult to pronounce them correctly.

Those who have studied a foreign language will easily understand this issue; writing is possible, but making the foreign language pronunciation exactly like a native speaker is extremely difficult. For example, in Vietnamese, some foreigners who have studied Vietnamese for a while can also speak Vietnamese to communicate with us, but as soon as they speak, we immediately notice the difference because their pronunciation is slurred and inaccurate.

Moreover, the written characters of Sanskrit are completely different from Chinese characters, and completely different from the Latin-based Vietnamese script.

So how can people from other countries like China, Japan, and Vietnam, with written scripts completely different... use their own characters to record mantras, yet when read aloud, sound like the original Sanskrit mantras to be widely transmitted?

It's a rather puzzling problem. Faced with this issue, the Great Masters responsible for spreading Buddhist mantras into other languages used one method, which is to use characters that have the closest pronunciation to the Sanskrit words in the mantra, assembling them into a version called a transliteration.

However, the transcription can never be 100% identical to the original Sanskrit version; there is always a certain degree of deviation.

For example, the Chinese use pictographic characters for writing. When transcribing a mantra, it is impossible to find a character that completely matches the pronunciation of the Sanskrit version, so one has to substitute it with a character that has a similar sound. In this way, the transcription (please note, transcription, not translation) will produce a mantra written in Chinese characters, which, when read aloud, sounds somewhat similar to the Sanskrit original, also called the romanized version.

Then, this transliterated version in Chinese was spread to Vietnam. Again, there was a similar problem when transcribing, as Vietnamese people use Latin characters as their writing system, making it impossible to use Vietnamese letters to create a transliteration that matches 100% with the Chinese version.

So the monks assigned with the mission of translation had to rewrite it into a Vietnamese transliteration, reading it according to the Chinese version, which was originally a transliteration from Sanskrit.

Why didn't he transliterate directly from Sanskrit into Vietnamese? Perhaps simply because at that time the Sanskrit version could not be found, or the translator was only specialized in Chinese rather than Sanskrit. (Many Vietnamese scriptures are translated from Chinese into Vietnamese, not from Sanskrit.)

It is precisely because of this transliteration – reading variation, that for the same mantra, each country reads it differently; no version is exactly the same, one has to listen carefully, very carefully, to find the similarities.

As a very common word in mantras, especially in the Great Compassion Mantra, repeated up to 14 times, it is the word "སྭཱ་ ཧཱ" – "Svaha". According to the Chinese transliteration reading, it is pronounced similar to "Sa pô hô." From this Chinese transliteration reading, Venerable Thich Thien Tam (1926-1992) transliterated it into Vietnamese – in the Latin alphabet – as the word "Ta Bà Ha."

Even the same transliteration in Vietnamese can have differences, for example, some versions are recorded as "Ta Bà Ha", while others are recorded as "Tát Bà Ha". Both readings are transliterations from the Chinese version, so it cannot be said that one version is correct and the other is wrong.

However, the Vietnamese quốc ngữ script has an advantage that few writing systems have, which is writing according to pronunciation, or colloquially, "write as you read," and nowadays, with technological development, we can easily find the Sanskrit version of a mantra online. So there is another way, which is to directly transcribe from Sanskrit to Vietnamese without going through the Chinese transliteration. In this way, the word Svaha can be written as "Xoa Ha" or "Soa Ha."

A question arises: Why not translate the meaning of the mantra?

Mantras are different from sutras; sutras can be translated for meaning, but mantras cannot, for many reasons. For example, each word contains too many meanings. The word "Ta Bà Ha" (Svaha) simultaneously encompasses many meanings: accomplishment – auspiciousness – perfection – dispelling misfortune – increasing benefit – non-abidance. Translating one meaning loses the others, and there are even profound meanings that only the Buddha fully understands. All of these are condensed into short mantra phrases. Beings only need to recite them, and even without understanding, they receive countless benefits. Therefore, when chanting, we only recite using the transliteration, not the translated meaning.

This is similar to taking medicine. We don’t need to be specialist pharmacists, knowing exactly how many chemical components are in the pill or how each component affects the body; we just follow the doctor's instructions and take it to get better.

The function of mantras, also called Dharani, or sacred utterances, is similar: one may not understand them, but still receives immense benefits. The evidence is that tens of thousands of people over thousands of years have recited the Great Compassion Mantra, or other mantras, without fully understanding the meaning of the words in them, not knowing what "Om" or "Ta Ba Ha" signifies, yet they still chant it and continue to receive enormous benefits.

This person recited the mantra to be cured of illness, another person recited the mantra and their temperament changed from violent to gentle, from ignorance to wisdom, etc.... Countless real-life miraculous responses serve as evidence for these mantras, which is why these mantras have been able to be maintained, preserved, passed down from generation to generation, continuously for several thousand years without being lost, spreading from one country to another up to the present day.

There are also many people who refute, including reputable Buddhist monks. They present all kinds of sharp arguments to counter the mantras, such as saying that when reciting sutras one must understand the meaning, or flatly denying that the Buddha taught these mantras (it is unknown whether they lived at the same time as the Buddha to hear all his words, yet they declare it very confidently), etc. But REALITY IS THE MOST VALUABLE ANSWER.

People can use sharp reasoning, which sounds very logical and persuasive, to make others believe in a certain point of view. However, in REALITY, if one or more events occur that contradict that point of view, the 'seemingly convincing' view immediately collapses completely and is buried by time into oblivion.

In reality, over the past several thousand years, despite many people not believing and providing various arguments against it, there have always been numerous, even extremely numerous, individuals who, by reciting mantras, achieved unimaginable benefits. Therefore, the mantras of the Buddha or of the Bodhisattvas preached in the sutras have continued to be widely transmitted, reaching distant countries, and even developing into one of the three largest sects in Buddhism, which is Vajrayana.

Returning to the issue of chanting mantras, if it is mispronounced and no longer resembles the original Sanskrit, does the person chanting still gain any benefits?

In fact, the answer is YES; many eminent masters, such as Venerable Hsuan Hua, have affirmed this.

Even when mispronounced, one can still achieve many of the functions and benefits of the mantra. Vietnamese people read the mantra in Vietnamese phonetic transcription, Chinese people read the mantra in the Chinese mispronunciation... it still works, still brings extraordinary miracles, and the hundreds of true stories that Quang Tu has published are concrete evidence of this.

Because whether reciting a mantra achieves any effect depends on many factors, and correct pronunciation is only one of them; additionally, the results also depend on the level of sincerity, the degree of faith, the level of moral discipline, the individual's aptitude, the method of practice, etc.

For example, Venerable Master Hsuan Hua is a typical example. He was Chinese and recited the Great Compassion Mantra using a Chinese distorted pronunciation, yet he was still able, through it, to open wisdom, attain supernatural powers, use the mantra to heal people, and perform many other abilities, gaining a world-renowned reputation.

____________________

There is a true story in Tibet that shows us that even if one mispronounces words while reciting mantras, if one can use the most sincere heart and does not generate doubt, one will definitely achieve unimaginable benefits:

At the border of Tây Khương province near Tibet, there lived an elderly woman in solitude; her husband and only son had passed away. She survived by cultivating a small plot of land with cereal grains. Having endured many hardships since childhood, the elderly woman felt that the karmic burdens within her were very heavy, so she diligently sought advice from those around her on methods to pray for peace of mind.

Finally, she was taught a mantra of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva by a kind pilgrim. The mantra consists of six syllables, Om Mani Padme Hum, which can be used to dispel karma obstacles.

Poor elderly village woman, she was illiterate, so on the way home she muttered to herself trying to memorize it, but she remembered it incorrectly and mispronounced it as Om Mani Padme Xanh.

To encourage the recitation of this repentance mantra, she set out two bowls, one empty and the other filled with soybeans. Each time she finished reciting a mantra, she would pick a bean from the full bowl and put it into the empty bowl, reversing the process once the empty bowl was full.

The old woman did not stop and sincerely chanted continuously for 30 years.

Her sincerity had manifested, so later the beans no longer needed her hand to pick them up; with each chant uttered, a bean would automatically jump into the neighboring bowl.

The old woman saw the beans jumping on their own, resonating with the tone of the chant, and realized that her practice was on the right path, so she became even more enthusiastic in her recitation.

One day, a high-ranking monk from Tibet was traveling through the area. When he passed by her shabby straw hut, he saw a radiant glow emanating from it.

This high-ranking monk was astonished; he thought that inside the straw hut there must be an accomplished spiritual practitioner. He hurriedly went in to pay a visit.

The old woman was delighted to see the monk visiting; she knelt down to pay her respects, while her mouth continued to mumble the mantra "Om Mani Padme Hum."

The monk was surprised, not understanding where the radiant aura he saw outside was coming from.

He gradually inquired:

-I wonder how many years the young lady has been cultivating, and is there anyone else here?

-Sir, I have been living alone here for more than thirty years.

-How pity, living alone must be very lonely?

-Not at all, even though I live alone, I practice cultivation and chant sutras every day so that in the next life I can enjoy much of the merits from this life; thanks to this, I don’t feel sad. Especially since a kind person taught me the way of cultivation, I have become even braver to live on.

-Which sutra are you practicing?

-Sir, I am illiterate, so I only recite a single mantra: Om Mani Padme Blue.

The monk sighed regretfully:

-Old lady, you have been reciting that mantra incorrectly. It should be pronounced Om Mani Padme Red.

At this moment, the old lady realized that she had been reciting the wrong mantra for over thirty years.

She was very saddened by this grave mistake, as it made her 30 years of chanting seem like sand cast into the Eastern Sea. However, she also thanked the monk for the correction.

- Anyway, you corrected it just in time, otherwise I would have continued to be wrong without knowing when I could adjust it correctly.

The monk bid the old lady farewell to continue his path of preaching.

The old lady resumed her chanting work, this time with the new mantra Án Ma Ni Bát Di Hồng.

However, her mind was still chaotic because of the recent events, so her will was not focused.

Each of her chants no longer made the beans excitedly jump into the next bowl as they used to. As the old woman chanted, tears kept falling, and she silently lamented that more than thirty years of cultivation work seemed to be flowing away like water because she had recited the spell incorrectly.

The monk walked a certain distance, then looked back and saw that the old woman's house no longer radiated a bright glow. Now the thatched hut appeared dilapidated and gloomy. The monk was startled and thought that it was he who had harmed this Buddhist follower, making her unable to concentrate as before. He hurried back to the thatched hut and said to the old woman:

- Just now I was only joking with you; your chant is actually the correct one.

- But why did master deceive me like that?

- I just wanted to see how sincere your devotion to the Triple Gem is. From now on, you can continue chanting as you always have; that is proper.

- Thank you, Buddha. I thought that my 30 years of chanting had gone in vain. I am grateful to master for teaching me.

After the monk left, the old lady resumed her chanting. With each recitation of the mantra "Om Mani Padme Hum," her heart felt joyful and a bean would automatically jump into the nearby bowl.

The monk climbed to the top of the mountain, and when he turned his head to look back, he saw a halo emanating from the old woman's thatched hut, lighting up the entire corner of the sky.

______________

However, to say that chanting according to a variant pronunciation can achieve 100% of the efficacy of the standard Sanskrit version is not possible. Because correct pronunciation still unleashes the mantra's power more strongly. Tibetan monks specializing in Tantra even have to spend many days and months training to be able to accurately pronounce each word in the mantra; it is not simple.

Yet, for some reason, if we can only chant the mantra according to these variant pronunciations, we still gain immense benefits.

Let me introduce to you a mantra that has the power to compensate for incorrect, incomplete, mispronounced recitations, or wrong tones, and also greatly increases the merits of the previous recitations. In addition, regularly reciting this mantra will help atone for sins, reduce illnesses, heal diseases quickly, and at the end of life, one will see the Buddha. (Recite 7 times at the end of the chanting session)

COMPENSATORY TRUE MANTRA:

OM HU RU HU RU GIA GIA MU KHÊ XOA HA

Even if my own strength cannot fully exert the full tenfold power of the mantra, achieving only nine parts, eight parts, or even just one percent, it still brings immeasurable merit.

Thanks to this, my karmic obstacles are eliminated, my virtues increase, worldly life and the Dharma are both fulfilled, and the seeds of Bodhi are sown for countless future lives, leading one day to the attainment of the supreme Bodhi enlightenment.

I wish everyone to always diligently practice, keep your spiritual mind steadfast, and soon accomplish Buddhahood!

Source: fb Quang Tử

tieu_de: LUST IS THE ROOT OF BIRTH AND DEATH SUFFERING
tom_tat: (HT Tuyen Hoa talks about the reincarnation of two trees) "The greatest harm in life is deep love."
noi_dung:
LUST IS THE ROOT OF SUFFERING AND BIRTH AND DEATH

(Venerable Tuyen Hoa lecturing about reincarnation of two tree trunks)

"The most harmful thing in life is deep love.

The noblest endeavor is to practice the pure path."

You see that this tree trunk consists of two branches, paired together as one, the upper branch combined with the lower branch. Do you know what this is? This is because countless lifetimes ago, there was a man and a woman who deeply loved each other. They made a vow: "In heaven, we wish to be like two wings of a bird. On earth, we wish to be like branches of the same tree." It means that if born in heaven, they would be a pair of lovers with joined wings, and if born on earth, they would wish to be the trunk and branches of the same tree. This man and woman were very faithful to each other, so they became husband and wife. Both shared the same interest, which was: love of money. The man risked his life to earn money, while the womanlikes to spend money wastefully, so give and take is completely reasonable and agreeable.

However, because their love was so intense, it created very deep suffering as well. Lifetimes after lifetimes, they were born into misery, falling into the path of animals, becoming hungry ghosts, and eventually descending into hell. Up to now, this couple has turned into vegetation. The base of this tree should have had two branches, but it grew from the same spot, so they are forever bound together and cannot separate. Do you see it? The left branch wraps around the right branch, and the right branch also bends to embrace the left branch, just like a man and a woman hugging each other. This shows that this man and woman had a habit of obsessive love, deeply entangled over many lowly lifetimes. TodayThey became a type of herb but still could not give up that desire. Between these two roots, there is a stone, which the two of them treasure like a jewel. What is that stone? It turns out it was the bank account passbook of the two of them in a previous life.

A few years ago, we once went into the city to give a Dharma talk. When passing by the riverbank, we saw this tree root and immediately picked it up and brought it home. Take a look: the top of this tree root was cut off, and the roots were also cut away, exposing two very dry branches, yet these two branches still continuously embrace each other. Don't you see that as pitiful?

Thus, it is clear that the deeper the love, the more dangerous it is. This is not something to joke about. Some people may think: "Teacher! I can't believe what you are saying about this Dharma, because it has no proof, it's not reasonable. Maybe you just want to scare children or speak in dreams." Whether you believe it or not is up to you; I have no way to make you believe because this Dharma is very difficult to explain, hard to talk about. Those who are enamored with desire, no matter how I explain, still will not awaken, will not accept it. The most harmful thing in life is deep love. The highest achievement is to cultivate a pure path. NotIt is true that people do not understand that principle; they know it but deliberately violate it because there is no way to break the habit formed in many previous lifetimes.

A Chinese proverb says: "Once your hand is holding a dry piece of firewood, it is difficult to let it go in exchange for a flower branch." This is meant to illustrate those who are always attached to worldly love. If one tells them to abandon such attachments to cultivate the Way, which is more valuable, they will surely stubbornly refuse to turn back. That is:

Heaven's rain, though gentle, seldom nourishes rootless grass.

Buddha's teachings, though vast, rarely save those without faith.

The meaning is:

The sky rains water everywhere, yet it is difficult to nourish plants without roots.

Although the Buddha's gate is vast and spacious, it is still hard to save those who have no faith.

I have preserved this tree root for many years. There are many people I did not want to show it to because even if I told them about this dharma, they would not believe it. I had to wait for the right moment, for it to ripen, before I spoke. On October 24, you all came from far and wide to pay respects, and I brought this tree root to the Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall. However, it was not until three weeks later that I spoke about it because if I did not, there might not be any more time. So, regardless of whether you believe it or not, I will still tell you the story of this tree root.

Master Hsuan Hua (Evening lecture on November 12, 1982 at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas - Dharmasite)

Two tree trunks are currently preserved at Vo Nguyen Duong Van Phat Thanh Thanh.

tieu_de: WHY ONE SHOULD NOT KILL
tom_tat: Please remember an ancient story in history, the day when King Tỳ Lưu Ly exterminated the Shakya family, even the Buddha's head suffered severe pain. What was the cause? It was in a distant past lifetime, when the Shakya family were the people
noi_dung:
WHY ONE SHOULD NOT KILL

Please remember an old story in history: the day King Ty Luu Ly killed the entire Shakya family, the Buddha also suffered a severe headache. What was the cause? In a distant past life, when the Shakya family were just fishermen and the Buddha Shakyamuni was a boy in that fishing village. When the fishermen caught a big fish, about to kill it for food, the young Bodhisattva playfully hit it on the head three times. That big fish was actually the previous life of King Luu Ly, who, when born as a human, killed the entire Shakya family, while the Buddha only repaid a mild consequence by having a headache.

You cannot help but believe this! The retribution is very clear and frightening. For this reason, the Buddha strictly forbade killing.

Not only is the Buddha compassionate toward humans, but He also cares for even the tiny insects. In the Buddha's view, all sentient beings can become Buddhas. In the Brahmajala Sutra, it is said: "All men are fathers, all women are mothers." Sentient beings go through the cycle of the six realms, having once been each other's parents and relatives. Therefore, killing sentient beings is considered equivalent to killing one's own parents.

People do not know or believe in this theory, so they freely kill and devour each other. You need to deeply believe in karma. If you deeply believe in karma, then even if your mind has not been transformed, goodness has already formed, because every time you act or think, you are always careful and deliberate, so actions will naturally follow the path of goodness.

Those who often encounter accidents do so because of evil karma, triggered by specific karma. One must understand that the disasters that occur are due to the evil deeds they have sown in the past. Therefore, accidents involving weapons, wars, floods, fires, earthquakes—all arise from ripened karma; it is the time for them to manifest, so one must accept them.

Good deeds bring good results! The proof is that in the last two World Wars, only Chinese people in Australia remained safe. Why? Because in their previous lives, they never created the karma of killing!

In the year of Giáp Dần (1914), I was teaching scriptures at Long Hoa Mountain when an earth-shattering earthquake occurred in the four districts of Dai Ly Prefecture, with the strongest impact in Dai Ly itself: all houses and city walls collapsed at once, leaving nothing behind. Only monasteries, temples, and stupas remained unharmed, standing as before. During the earthquake, the ground shook and cracked severely, and fierce fires broke out and spread everywhere. As people scrambled to escape the disaster, the earth suddenly split open beneath their feet, causing them to fall in and get trapped. They tried their utmost to climb out, but just as they managed to emerge, the ground would close again, severing heads and leaving them stuck in the soil. The terrifying scene resembledpeople who are alive but are trapped in hell being chopped or burned by fire, so tragic that it is unbearable to look at.

Thousands of households in the city perished, with very few survivors. There are two gold shops here: Vạn Xương shop owned by the Triệu family and Trạm Nhiên shop owned by the Dương family – when the fire reached the homes of these two families, it immediately went out. Their place of residence was also not affected by the earthquake. Each household had only a few dozen people, but all of them were safe and unharmed. The reason is that these two families have, for generations, observed vegetarianism and often practiced charity and almsgiving, which is why they were able to attract such a rare blessing. Anyone who knows about this story also feels moved.

As Buddhists, you must thoroughly understand this complex law of cause and effect and have unwavering faith in it. If you deeply believe in cause and effect, you will voluntarily do good deeds, observe precepts, maintain a pure vegetarian lifestyle, and no longer dare to take life.

Venerable Hư Vân

(Excerpt from Báo Ứng iện Đời 6 - Hạnh Đoan)
